name: Garcinia cambogia
lead: Garcinia cambogia, now classified as Garcinia gummi-gutta, is a tropical fruit tree native to the Western Ghats of southwestern India. Its fruit rind is used as a sour flavouring in curries, and its principal acid, hydroxycitric acid (HCA), is extracted and sold as a weight-loss dietary supplement.[1][2]

HCA inhibits the enzyme ATP-citrate lyase in laboratory work, which led to claims that it could lower fat synthesis.[3] A 12-week randomised controlled trial in JAMA tested the extract for body weight and fat mass, and systematic reviews of weight-loss supplements have generally rated the evidence as weak.[4][5][6] Cases of liver injury have been reported with multi-ingredient supplements that contained it.[7]

paras: Garcinia gummi-gutta is a tree up to about 20 metres whose pumpkin-shaped fruit is used as a souring agent in Indian and Thai cooking. Ayurvedic tradition associates sour flavours with digestion; ethnobotanical uses include remedies for bowel complaints.[1][2] HCA is the compound most associated with the species.[1][3]

(-)-HCA is a potent inhibitor of ATP-citrate lyase, which supplies acetyl-CoA for fatty acid synthesis.[3] Animal work reported that HCA administration in mice spared carbohydrate use and promoted lipid oxidation during exercise.[8]

A 1998 JAMA randomised trial in overweight adults evaluated Garcinia cambogia for body weight and fat mass over 12 weeks.[4] Later reviews of dietary supplements and herbal medicines for obesity have examined it among other products and generally describe weak or inconsistent evidence.[5][9] A 2015 review describes its popularity as a weight-loss supplement.[2] Reference works note that it was promoted by a US television doctor in 2012.[1]

Reported effects include dry mouth, nausea, stomach discomfort and headache, and a 2011 meta-analysis found gastrointestinal events about twice as common as with placebo.[1] Liver toxicity has been reported with Hydroxycut, a product containing the extract,[1] and tabulations of hepatotoxic supplements list Garcinia-containing products.[7] A systematic review has examined adverse events of herbal weight-loss supplements.[10] Reference works note possible interactions with diabetes, asthma and clotting medicines.[1]

Garcinia extracts appear as ingredients in homeopathic weight-loss products. One US label states its claims are based on traditional homeopathic practice, are not accepted medical evidence and are not FDA evaluated.[11]

Human trials include a 12-week JAMA randomised controlled trial of Garcinia cambogia in overweight adults,[4] and trials of Garcinia species have been included in systematic reviews and meta-analyses of herbal weight-loss products.[5][9] Registered trials of related Garcinia species (such as mangosteen) address other conditions.[12]

timeline.event: JAMA randomised trial of Garcinia cambogia for weight loss published.[4]
Promoted on US television as a natural weight-loss aid, per reference sources.[1]

card.summary: HCA-based fat-burner supplement; trials and reviews mostly find weak effects, with some liver-injury reports in blended products.
card.aka: Garcinia gummi-gutta, HCA, brindle berry, Malabar tamarind
card.note: Liver toxicity has been reported with multi-ingredient products containing the extract.

quick.overview:
Garcinia cambogia is a tropical fruit whose rind contains hydroxycitric acid (HCA), sold as an over-the-counter weight-loss supplement.

A 1998 JAMA trial and later systematic reviews of weight-loss supplements describe limited or inconsistent evidence of benefit.
quick.mechanism: In the lab, HCA inhibits ATP-citrate lyase, an enzyme involved in making fatty acids, which is the basis for claims that it reduces fat storage.
quick.risks: Reported effects include nausea, stomach discomfort, headache and dry mouth. Liver toxicity has been reported with products containing the extract, and it may interact with some medicines.
